Triggers.value: Feeling physically restrained or held down

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Going to or near the place where the event happened
I try hard to control my emotions

Threat.value: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day

Memory.value: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.

issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Needles/Medical): Medical equipment such as needles or drips
issues.explanation: These triggers are hard to reconcile with the stated trauma of physical abuse by a romantic partner. 'Feeling restrained or held down' fits well, but medical equipment and helicopter sounds suggest a medical, combat, or accident context that is not represented in the Threat, Memory, Appraisals, or Strategy items.

issues.item: Triggers: Auditory (Helicopter): Helicopter or aircraft sounds
issues.explanation: Because Triggers has strong links to Threat and Memory in the formulation, the trigger content should plausibly connect to the patient's danger cues and trauma memories. The profile's Threat items center on interpersonal hypervigilance in close environments (silence, nearby movement, lock checking), and Memory items do not contain medical or aircraft content, making these two triggers clinically incoherent with the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Triggers: Auditory (Helicopter): Helicopter or aircraft sounds
issues.explanation: 'Helicopter or aircraft sounds' is hard to reconcile with the stated trauma type of physical abuse by a romantic partner unless there is additional undisclosed trauma exposure; it does not fit the rest of the profile, which centers on interpersonal/domestic threat cues such as restraint, doors, movement, and lock checking.

issues.item: Threat: Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
issues.explanation: 'Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen' is not impossible, but paired with the otherwise specifically interpersonal/domestic cue pattern it weakens coherence because it suggests a different threat context without support from memory or appraisal items.

vignette:
Mateo Alvarez, a 37-year-old social ministry worker, sought treatment more than a year after the end of an abusive relationship that had unfolded largely behind the doors of the apartment he had once shared with his former partner. The worst assaults happened at night after his partner had been drinking. Mateo could still picture one episode with painful clarity: the smell of alcohol on his partner’s breath filling the small hallway, the apartment door slamming hard enough to shake the frame, and then being shoved onto the couch and pinned by the wrists while he went rigid under the other man’s weight. What stayed with him was not only the fear but the humiliation and grief of realizing, even in the moment, that someone he had loved was hurting him. Since leaving, he had refused to go near that building. He told himself there was no reason to pass that block, but the thought of the entrance, the stairwell, even the sound of a heavy door in a nearby corridor was enough to make his body lock up and his face go blank as he fought to keep any feeling from showing.

In the months afterward, the ordinary settings of his work began to feel unpredictable. Mateo spent his days moving between parish offices, community rooms, and clients’ homes, and he noticed how often doors opened suddenly behind him in those spaces. A volunteer pushing into an office, a client entering a meeting room too quickly, or the sharp slam of a church side door could make him jolt as if he were about to be grabbed. If someone brushed past him in a narrow hallway, he reacted to the movement before he could think, his shoulders tensing and his breath stopping. The smell of alcohol on a congregant after an evening event could do the same. Those moments did more than unsettle him; they brought back the apartment with startling immediacy, and in his mind he could hear the same slammed door and the same drunken voice from the assaults as though the scene were happening again.

Because he had come to expect danger in these flashes, Mateo increasingly organized his life around preventing them. At night he moved through his own apartment checking the locks on the front door and windows over and over, unable to settle until he had reassured himself again. Night felt especially unsafe to him, the hour when he was most certain something could happen without warning. When startled by movement nearby, he found himself freezing completely, the same immobilized response that had overtaken him during the abuse, and afterward he would clamp down hard on any sign of fear or sadness. He worked to keep his voice even, his expression controlled, and his body still, convinced that if he let himself feel what was there it would overwhelm him. This effort to stay tightly contained narrowed his world: he lingered less after evening ministry events, avoided unfamiliar apartments when possible, and made excuses to colleagues when meetings were scheduled near the neighborhood where he had lived with his ex-partner.

Yet the more he tried not to feel or remember, the more piercing the memories became. When something set him off, Mateo did not just have a vague recollection; he had intensely clear, detailed images of the couch fabric, the pressure on his wrists, the angle of the hallway light. Along with the images came sound. He sometimes heard, in his head, the violent crack of the door and fragments of his partner’s voice as if they were echoing in the room around him. What hit him most forcefully on recall was grief—grief for the relationship he thought he had, grief for how long he had stayed, grief for the version of himself who had believed he could calm things down if he kept control. That grief made him redouble his efforts to shut everything down, but the emotional constriction seemed only to leave the memories sealed off and vivid, ready to be reawakened by the next slammed door or the next trace of alcohol on someone’s breath.

Over time, the memories themselves made the world feel full of cues. After a night of poor sleep and repeated lock-checking, he would enter work already scanning for doors, bodies moving too close, any smell that resembled beer or liquor. In that keyed-up state, even neutral moments registered as warnings. And once he had frozen in front of a colleague or quietly stepped out of a room to regain control, the incident confirmed for him that he was still vulnerable, still one sound or one movement away from being back there. What finally brought Mateo to treatment was a recent evening meeting at the parish center when a maintenance worker swung open a door behind him and the odor of alcohol from a guest in the hallway hit him at the same time. Mateo went completely still, heard the old door slam in his head, and had to leave before he could speak. He was ashamed that his work now revolved around avoiding places and managing himself, but what frightened him most was the sense that nights, doors, and other people’s movements were steadily taking over his life. He said he wanted help because he could not keep living as if every room might become that apartment again.
